utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Madam Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Allow me, Mr. Prosecutor and Mr. Hayman, before continuing with your witness, to indicate that today is our last day for the month of August, and we will conclude work at 5.45. The afternoon will begin at 3.00, so I would like both sides to seek to end work today at a convenient point. I think we are meeting again on 24th September. I wish to remind you that the Appeals Chamber is going to deal with an appeal, the appeal of Croatia in this same case of Blaskic, the question of subpoenas. That is what I am asking, that at 5.45, we interrupt the proceedings at a coherent point in the case. That is all. Mr. Prosecutor, you can have your witness brought in, Mr. Kavazovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning Mr. President, your Honours, counsel. At the conclusion of yesterday's session, your Honour, one housekeeping matter I would like to bring to the court's attention, and that is Mme. Fauveau brought to my attention that when I had asked Mr. Kavazovic to circle the SDK building in the colour pink on Prosecutor's exhibit 45C, he marked the SDK building and circled it in the colour orange. For the record, the Prosecutor's exhibit 45C has orange markings circling the SDK building and the initials SDK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you Mme. Fauveau for your vigilance and for indicating the mistake in the colour used. Please have Mr. Sulejman Kavazovic brought in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kavazovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. You are still under oath and you will continue to be questioned by the Prosecution whose witness you are. SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask the usher initially, your Honour, to please place on the easel Prosecutor's exhibit 45C. While that exhibit is being placed on the easel, Mr. Kavazovic, at the conclusion of yesterday's testimony, you brought to my attention an error that you had made on Prosecutor's exhibit 45C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I made an error. I marked a position below the road, a couple of centimetres to the left instead of to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I approach that exhibit? I cannot see that exhibit because of the fold on the left side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Harmon. Of course, if the Defence wants to approach, it is welcome to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, it should be exhibit 56C that should be mounted. Mr. Usher, if you would take that clip on the left-hand side top and move that, because it covers the marking made by the witness. Mr. Kavazovic, can you explain the error and can you correct it on the Prosecution's exhibit 56C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. I can correct the error, and indicate the error that I have made. I made the error here, because I was digging trenches not to this side of the road, but on the other side of the road, so this is wrong and this is right. This is where I was digging the dugout in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you take the dark pen that is in front of you and cross out the pink mark on the left where you have made the error? Thank you, Mr. Kavazovic, you can have a seat. For the record, your Honour, the pink mark on prosecutor's exhibit 56C on the right is where Mr. Kavazovic was digging trenches. Mr. Kavazovic, you indicated that while you were on the front lines in Kratine, you saw the military police, the MUP, the HVO and the Jokers working along those lines. Did it appear to you that those units were working together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were working together since they were in the same area. They were linked one to another along the same line, so they were working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I can ask the usher to please place on the easel Prosecutor's exhibit 29G. Mr. Kavazovic, could you approach Prosecutor's exhibit 29G and mark the area of Kratine where you were digging trenches? Could you use a pink pen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the area where I was digging trenches, Kratine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can remain standing there for one minute. Mr. Usher, I am going to ask that one additional image be placed on the easel. It will be Prosecutor's exhibit 51C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I ask you? I missed something. You asked whether the HVO and the Jokers were working together with someone; who was the third?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The HVO, the Jokers, the MUP and the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We do not have a document 51C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What is the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Kavazovic to explain what the MUP is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The MUP stands for the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It is the civilian police, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, MUP. The civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I ask that that exhibit be marked as Prosecutor's exhibit -- is it C?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be 51A.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, could you take a look at Prosecutor's exhibit 51A and can you locate any particular trenches on that photograph that you dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph, I can see the trenches that were dug by us, the imprisoned civilians. These were the trenches used by the Croatian fighters and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you please mark those trenches with the colour pink.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bungalow at Nadioci, so from Nadioci we went to Kratine, this is Kratine, and we were digging trenches here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the centre of that circle you have drawn, does one of the trenches that you dug appear to be visible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Here it is. You can see the trenches; you can see the path. They could not pass, so we had to dig the trenches so they would not be hit by the Territorial Defence and the Defence forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kavazovic. You can have a seat. I would ask that the usher please place on the ELMO Prosecutor's exhibit 29C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Prosecutor, and I address myself to the Defence as well when their time comes, to give notice to the Registrar of the exhibits that you will need in the necessary order: "I will ask for exhibit 50, then 29", et cetera; which will save us some time. Continue please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, can you take a look at Prosecutor's exhibit 29C and can you, in looking at that exhibit, inform the court how far away Kratine is from the hotel Vitez. First of all, can you point to Kratine. (Witness indicates). How far away is that from the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The distance from the hotel Vitez is 5 to 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Usher. I am finished with that exhibit. Mr. Kavazovic, while you were at the front lines during the seven to eight days that you said you were there, did you have an opportunity to see any communications equipment in the possession of the HVO units that were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there, Mr. Ivica Vujica, the commander of a part of the Jokers, had radio equipment on him from the former JNA. It is a green radio receiver which is carried over the shoulder. It has an earphone on the side; I do not know exactly the time or model, but it is a radio receiver and transmitter and he used it, he spoke over it. I saw that others who were also commanders and leaders of platoons and detachments carried these Motorolas or radio stations as a means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said a portable Motorola. Did you see a portable telephone as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is at the same time a telephone. It is actually a radio station, some kind of radio. It was green with a shoulder strap, and I think it is equipment of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Mr. Kavazovic, that the units at that line were able to communicate with each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did communicate in fact. When I reached Ivica Vujica, commander of the Jokers -- he is from Busovaca -- he was called up over this radio. The words were "Idol is calling Sardina", which is probably some kind of code language used in radio communication, and the question was, "Idol have you received men for digging?" He answered, "Sardina, yes, I have got the men." I do not know who was Idol and who was Sardina but those were the words used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, based on that conversation, that units on the enemy line were able to communicate with units behind that particular line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, while you were at that particular line for those number of days, were you threatened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were threats. We had to do what we were told. We did not dare, of course, run away. There was always a guard, depending on where we were digging. If we were digging at the HVO lines, one of the soldiers would stand by, armed, and he would threaten, "Do not dare try and run because we will kill you all", so we had to have our heads bowed looking downwards. Rarely were we allowed to look elsewhere, where we were not supposed to look, so we had to do heavy labour. We had to dig for a whole day sometimes. Once I had to dig a rock to remove the rock so that it would serve as a shield for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you ever forced to place mines in the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion, actually on the fourth or fifth day, Mr. Anto Furundzija came amongst the eight of us, together with four members. Two belonged to the HVO and two were Jokers, like Anto Furundzija himself, who was a Joker. Then he asked which one of us knew how to lay mines. We were all silent. Then he asked again, "Does anyone know who is a pyrotechnician", that is persons dealing with explosives, who understand explosives. We all bowed our heads and nobody gave any answer. Then he pointed at me and said, "Kavaz, you are coming with me." I was terrified; I wondered why me? Then I went to a stream where mines had to be laid. They were also JNA mines. He asked me whether I knew how to lay them and I said, "I have no idea." He told me to try. However, while working in the army as a corporal, I did come across these mines, but for training purposes, not combat. I knew the procedure for laying a minefield. So I started working on it. When I got the fuses, they were training lighters; the lighters were not the real ones. I do not know what the reason was. I told them that the difference between training lighters, which are yellow -- and the combat lighters are red. I explained to this man the difference, that it was not a lighter for combat mines. So he brought some others. I do not know whether they were doing this to check whether I knew how to do it or not, so I placed them there and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you lay those mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I laid the mines at Kratine on the left-hand side alongside a stream, along the dividing line between the HVO and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately what date, Mr. Kavazovic, did you leave the Kratine area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went around 30th April, the 28th or 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you leave the front lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having worked so hard -- I worked all the time; I had very little rest -- I could not eat fish. I just cannot stand it and throughout the period I was there I had to eat this fish. Sometimes I was forced to eat it. Being exhausted, I fainted, I lost consciousness, and upon the orders, or at least I heard that Bralo Mladen, Cicko, ordered that I be taken away from the area, and two of my comrades who were with me, captured civilians, were told to put me in a van and drive me to Busovaca and that is what they did. The same driver, known as Zabac, put me in this van, together with the two civilians Cengalovic Jasmin and Adnan Piric, I was driven to the first aid station at Busovaca, where I was given medical treatment, I got an injection and I came to. My muscles were stiff, I had serious inflammation of the muscles and both my legs and arms had gone stiff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you said Mladen Cicko, you mean Bralo, Miroslav Bralo, also known as Cicko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bralo Miroslav, known as Cicko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you were given this medical treatment, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After medical treatment -- they treated me correctly; I was given an infusion and an injection -- the same van waited for me and they took me back to Kaonik, the camp there at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher place the following exhibit which is a copy of the previous exhibit, number 59 on the easel, your Honour. I believe that will be Prosecutor's exhibit 59A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, exhibit number 59A.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, would you first of all take the pointer and can you point out where you were taken, where Kaonik is on that particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here these are shelters of the Territorial Defence of the former JNA warehouses, former military warehouses, and I was taken there from the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you take a pink pen and just put a circle around that location, please. You can have a seat again. After you were taken there by the HVO, where were you placed in that particular facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was placed in a building which had small premises about 2.5 metres long and 2 metres wide. They were warehouses, storage space, and these premises had numbers, so I was in room number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have access in and out of that room freely or were you guarded by somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rooms were locked. I was put in room number 5 and if I wanted to go out, I had to knock; there was an opening on the door. I would say, "Room number 5." Then he would ask me, "What do you want?" I would say, "I need to go to the toilet", he would open and accompany me to the toilet and bring me back. That was the only time we were outside. When I was given lunch, the door would be opened so that I could see while eating and then they would be closed again. In the camp, I was given two meals a day for the two days I was there. In the morning there was a cooked meal, cooked rice at 9.00, and at 4.00 again there was rice and potatoes, so anyway the food was much better than on the frontlines where we were digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you able to identify by particular military unit the guards that were guarding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards that were guarding us at the entrance were military policemen, and inside the building they were members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said you remained at Kaonik for two days. Where did you go after you left Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the third day, or rather the third day in the morning, Mr. Zabac came because he had promised that he would come for me the next day; he did not come the next day but the day after. He came with a van and two members of the HVO military police, and he drove me again to the SDK building, where I had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you arrived at the SDK building, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got to the SDK building, the people whom I had left behind were there, and then I met with people who had also been digging trenches like me, so we talked to each other, where we had been, where we had done the digging, and I was waiting for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did the people you talked to say they had been digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the conversations we had, and judging from the people who came to Kratine, I learned that people had been digging trenches in Krcevine, Dubravica, Sivrino Selo, from all the camps in Vitez; people were rounded up and taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many other detainees were with you in the SDK building at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 62. I was the 63rd. Anyway they were all there when I came back. There was eight of us, I was the ninth, that were taken away, but the others did not go anyway. We waited for the exchange which had been promised us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you in fact exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the exchange took place. The Red Cross came; they brought buses and then we went to sign statements there that we did not wish to stay in Vitez. Even the people who wanted to stay did not dare say so because the situation was terrible for Muslims under the control of the HVO, so that we all had no other choice but to say that we wanted to leave Vitez to go to Zenica or Travnik, somewhere where the BH-Army was in control, and then the Red Cross would call out the names individually. The HVO military policemen were there who took us out in groups of five. Then we waited to be called out and to sign this statement, that we did not want to live in Vitez but that we wanted to go to Zenica. This was not something that we wanted. I personally did not want to go to Zenica. I like Vitez, I prefer Vitez, but I was forced to leave Vitez and go to Zenica because if I had signed to say that I wanted to stay in Vitez, I would probably have been captured again or even something worse could have happened, because the Muslims in areas under Croatian control were insulted, mistreated, harassed, so that I had to sign this statement to say that I wanted to go to Zenica, that I did not want to live in Vitez. Then I got into this bus organised by the Red Cross. We were escorted by UNPROFOR and taken to the UNPROFOR base in Nova Bila. We waited there for three or four hours to be allowed passage to Zenica, because at the checkpoint near the railway station under the control of the HVO we were not allowed to pass. They wanted to search the buses, but the Red Cross would not allow it. They did not agree with that. So we had to wait for two hours for the commander of the UNPROFOR -- their names were Stewart and Anderson -- to come to an agreement with them to allow us to pass to Zenica. After two or three hours, I cannot remember exactly, the bus set off towards Vitez, the railway station, via Vjetrenice to Zenica, and that is how I got to Zenica. I gave the Red Cross the address I wanted to go to. The condition was that I must have some relatives in Zenica, to have an address there, to be able to leave Vitez. My wife had an uncle and I gave his name and address and that is how I managed to go to Zenica. So I could not leave Vitez unless I had someone in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic I am going to show you Prosecutor's next exhibit, which I would ask be marked Prosecutor's exhibit 99 and I am going to ask you to identify that in just a moment. Before you say anything about that, Mr. Kavazovic, first of all can you identify the document? Then I am going to ask you a question about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document of the Red Cross that we received once we were identified in Vitez, and after that, with these papers in the Red Cross office, we had our dates of birth et cetera sent to Zagreb and then these papers were sent back to us. However there is a problem with registration. 24th September 1993 is the date written here. However, I was taken out to dig trenches on the 22nd, and my father-in-law was at the SDK, then, when the Red Cross came to identify all these people who were in there and to register them and to make these lists, knowing my name, he gave my name. So that is how I was listed, and my place of birth and date of birth et cetera, and that is how these people who were there gave these data about us so that we could be registered with the Red Cross too. When I came to the SDK, when I was returned to the SDK on the 30th , or rather on 3rd May, I got a paper from the Red Cross which my father-in-law had actually filled out for me. I did not even see these Red Cross people, nor did I see any of this before. My father-in-law did all of this for me. This is the day they came to the SDK, but I was not there, I did not see anyone. Fortunately my father-in-law was there, so he got these papers for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, you may have mis-spoken, because on the transcript it says -- the line that says "was registered by ICRC delegates on ...", your testimony was "on 24th September 1993" and what is written there is "April 26th 1993". Do you see that? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 26th April 1993, that is when they made this registry of people in the SDK in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is the date that your father-in-law gave the Red Cross your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He gave my personal data, and on the basis of these personal data, he got the card that he obtained, so when I came, I got the card and I did not see any of these people myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, after you were released to the Red Cross, did you receive medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got out, I had to report to Dr Mujezinovic. I went to see him. In the evening when I would go to bed, I felt very stressful. I had heart trouble, probably because of everything that I had experienced. My courage had also gone down, so I went for treatment to Mujezinovic. It was not real treatment; I went to talk to him so he would encourage me, he would help me. He is a doctor of internal medicine and he is also good at psychology, so he recommended me to Dr Sestic, a neuropsychiatrist in Zenica. I went to see him several times and then from a psychological point of view he explained to me that it was only natural after everything that I had lived through -- that this would heal, but it would take a year or two for this fright of mine to disappear. It was only a normal reaction, he said, because all that time I was tense, I was afraid. Now I am fine, I have no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You saw Dr Mujezinovic at some point in time in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After your release from the Vitez area, did you join the Armija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a month and a half again I joined a formation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was appointed head of the transportation service in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you currently serving as a member of the Armija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am an active officer. I am a lieutenant. I am in charge of the transportation service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kavazovic. I have no additional questions of you but the Defence lawyers will be asking you some questions and the judges will be asking you some questions. Your Honours, I would ask to move into evidence the following Prosecutor's exhibits; 45C, 29G, 56C, 50C, 51A, 59A and 99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, no objection? No objection. Very well, Mme Fauveau, these exhibits will be admitted into evidence according to the statement of the Prosecutor. Now you are going to be asked a certain number of questions by the Defence counsel, the lawyers of General Blaskic. I do not know whether it is going to be Mr. Nobilo -- yes, it is Mr. Nobilo. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Kavazovic. As you have heard, I am Anto Nobilo, the attorney of General Blaskic and I would like to put a few questions to you. Tell me, in the JNA, you got a certain rank. Did you attend reserve officers' school or how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did my military service in Delnice in Croatia. I attended a course for corporals and after that, I completed my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you a reserve officer after that and were you asked to attend additional courses and exercises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Turbe once I went for exercises and that was all, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in 1992, you joined the Territorial Defence. I would like to know whether this was voluntary or were you called up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was voluntary, I was not called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reported in Vitez. Zenada Causev was the woman who was in charge of the people who were volunteering to join the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, you reported to Zenada. Did you immediately get a uniform and arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not have arms then. I was wearing civilian clothes and for about 15 days, we were coming in just like that in civilian clothes. We reported in, and at that time in Zljeme the Yugoslav People's Army were creating problems, they were supposed to leave warehouses so we were just told to report in every other day and that is what we would do, and then we would go back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you participate in the actions in Zljeme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you get an uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not get a real uniform. From Soko Mostar, we got blue overalls, I think from the airport. I do not know. We got this from Kresevo, so we got these overalls that are usually worn by aircraft mechanics. The Territorial Defence first had these blue uniforms, so it was not camouflage uniforms, but these were two-piece uniforms, overalls and matching blue jackets. That is all the Territorial Defence had until June, I think, from April to June. We wore them for about two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But otherwise in the Territorial Defence were uniforms a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So there were members who did not have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were first arrested by the HVO, you said that you were questioned about the Territorial Defence, and that you did not tell them anything; you did not know anything or you did not want to tell them anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not my responsibility. I simply was not responsible for that. I did not have any answers to give them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I do not understand. Did you know how to answer some of their questions and you did not want to answer them or did you simply not know how to give an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know how to answer some of these questions. I did not understand some of these questions. When they asked me what Territorial Defence was and why it was there, how could I explain that? How could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that you had a relatively important position already in 1992 in view of your age, that you were head of transportation? Can you tell me, in 1992, for example in the second half of 1992, how was the Territorial Defence in the municipality of Vitez organised? Where were its headquarters and what were the units that existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Vitez in 1992 were in the high school in Vitez, Boris Kidric high school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a staff platoon or someone else who was guarding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You do not know; you were the driver of Hakija Cengic right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I really do not know. I was not involved. I do not think there was that kind of platoon because we did not have uniforms. People asked for uniforms and we did not have any. We could not give them any, so we would come to Vitez, report in and then we would go back after two days as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is what you did say for the first half of 1992, but the second half, when you got those blue overalls, in the second half of 1992, was there a platoon that was protecting the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a battalion of the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a detachment of the TO in Visoko with Hakija Dzelilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there one in Preocica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a TO detachment in Poculice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have never heard of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard of Poculice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But the TO detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a TO detachment in Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dubravica, that means Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you whether it was there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there one in Hanka Panija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about Hanka Panija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you have already said, because you know the language, you are going very fast, but could you please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Certainly. Was there a TO detachment in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a TO detachment in Kolonija in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a TO detachment in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a TO detachment in Vraniska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a logistics centre of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Logistics centre of the Territorial Defence, yes. In the municipal headquarters in Vitez, in a private house, there was a logistics base, but it was not really a logistics base. Flour and food were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there weapons there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some weapons that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a communications unit then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Anti-aircraft platoon -- antisabotage platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Antisabotage platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As the head of transportation unit for the Territorial Defence, what was your task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As head of the transportation section, first of all I only had four vehicles. My task was to provide a vehicle when the Commander was supposed to go and talk to the HVO and he was supposed to attend joint meetings. I was the one who would have to take care of who would drive him when I stopped driving his vehicle; then I appointed two new drivers for him. They would alternate every other day. So when the Commander would have this meeting, for example he would tell me, "I have a meeting at the hotel Vitez and I need a vehicle to take me to the hotel Vitez." I had to make sure that the Commander could always have one of these four vehicles for his purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: These four cars, were all of them passenger cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a private van and there were two that belonged to the former joint Territorial Defence headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you do with the van? What did you transport in it and where did it go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When flour was supposed to be brought in, when food was supposed to be prepared, the van would go and collect that. We would simply carry out the Commander's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Food. Where did you bring food in from and where did you take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What place? From the store for instance from Princip we would get nine meals at one point in time. That is where the HVO also obtained their breakfast from, and if they did not have a vehicle to bring in the breakfast to the school or to another building, we would send our van in to bring in breakfast or lunch or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever drive the Commander to certain villages of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not get out of town at all while I was driving, and after that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But towards the end of 1992 when you became head of the transportation service, your drivers, did they go to some villages and other places in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think that you have as evidence these papers giving instructions where to go, for example Vitez Lokava; from the high school to his home, which was nearby, and then for example from the high school to the police department down there or to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we can conclude that you were head of the transportation service, your drivers, your vehicles were driving around Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that part of town and Stari Vitez for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it is within the town of Vitez. So that is the service you headed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right, thank you. You were the driver of the Commander. How many people were there in the headquarters of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that. I did not have access to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these people? Do you know some of the people who were members of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Sajic Jelko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the second half of 1992. I knew the Commander and I knew Zenada Causev.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you were head of the transportation service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was head of the transportation service. I am sorry, I knew my boss at logistics, but logistics is something different from the headquarters. There were different commanders at the headquarters and different commanders at logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right, I asked you about the headquarters, the staff. You knew two people. Tell me, this conflict in October in Ahmici, when that occurred, did you have any contact with someone from Ahmici or somebody else in your presence, either by radio or by telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not think so; I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You do not think so or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I simply do not know. At any rate, I know what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you: did someone in your presence speak over the radio with someone in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before the morning when you went to Visoko, when you were coming back from Ahmici, when were you coming back from Ahmici, at what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 1.30, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. At 1.30, was the conflict over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the conflict had only started. I got into the fire, I was passing through Ahmici, I saw one house burning, another house burning, a third house burning. I did not understand what was happening. When I came to Vitez people were standing there in uniforms, by the buildings, and I went to logistics. I managed to reach logistics and nobody stopped me, I do not know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear shooting when you were passing through Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see any roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a checkpoint but it was moved aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the morning, did you go to Visoko the same day when you came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you see in the morning as you were passing to Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw houses, normal houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a checkpoint there, a roadblock? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of tyres and also two rails from a railroad that were we welded together so that you cannot pass with a heavy truck; you cannot move very fast. That is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did somebody guard that roadblock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his name; I cannot remember it now. It was a member of the HVO, and also there was a similar roadblock at the railway station, so in Ahmici, a member of the HVO guarded this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was sitting there on a chair. I imagine he was guarding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So whose checkpoint was it, of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any offers to switch to the HVO at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who made the offer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Furundzija on one occasion told me that I could be transferred to the HVO, that I would have a higher salary, because our earnings were low. I cannot remember exactly. Those were the first BH dinars, very little anyway, and he told me, "Why do you not join with us? You will have a much better salary in Deutschemarks", but I did not want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why did you not? It is normal to go where you are better paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That depends on the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had my opinion. I did not think money was everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my private view; I do not think that big money seems so much. To this day I do not think it is everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you do not want to explain to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you have asked the same question four times. You have been given an answer. He answered your question. It is his point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to go on to another question. When you were arrested for the first time, was any reference made to this fact that you had refused to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time? A little bit, yes. Vlado Santic asked me why I would not joint the HVO and I had to say that I just did not want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that a general mobilisation was proclaimed and a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean. For the whole population or for certain segments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know that the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, the President of the whole state, had proclaimed a state of war and a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The day you saw the roadblock at Ahmici held by the HVO, which road did you take to Visoko from Vitez to Ahmici and from Ahmici -- where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to Lasva then Bila Selo (?), from Bilesevo to Kakanj, from Kakanj to Mostar and Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it not closer to take the road from Busovaca and Kiseljak to Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but you had to be able to pass along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a dangerous road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean there were potholes or curves or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a very dangerous road, there were lots of curves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that was the only reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why were you driving from Visoko to Vitez and what was -- which location in Visoko did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Mostre near Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was situated there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims were there who had gone there because the attack had started on Visoko. The JNA had attacked. They had attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina and I do not know under whose orders people were told to go there to be in a state of alert.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So obviously you went to take something there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go to take anything. I just went there by orders of the Commander to see whether any vehicles were necessary there, and on my way back to Visoko, the factory at Kovin -- I think it is a steel mill mostly -- the TO at the time had some shells, 120 millimetre, I think. I do not understand them very well, but they did not have additional charge and they were literally confiscated from the JNA without fuses and without additional charge and by orders of somebody called Mevludin from Breza. He was a commander there; I do not know his surname. Mevludin was his name. He told me to take that back to Vitez, to the Princip Selo factory so they can try and manufacture what was necessary. So I transported 34 or 35 shells, not I but people loaded these shells into the Fiat van that I was driving. It was in private property; it did not belong to the army. I do not remember the owner's name; the man was living in Germany and he lent it to the TO, so I loaded these shells and set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you picked up those shells by chance? Where did you take them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took them to the house where the logistics was. That is where I arrived with the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it just a van or was it a convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that when you arrived, the city was blocked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you imply when you say "blocked"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my view, when I say "blocked", it means when civilians do not walk the streets, when they are prohibited from walking, when there is only the military in the town, when civilians cannot move freely. I did not see a single civilian walking in town. The shops were not working, the cafes and restaurants were not working, it was not a Saturday or a Sunday, holiday day; it was a working day, as far as I remember. There were checkpoints: at Rijeka there was a checkpoint; this is a kind of blockade. There was a checkpoint at the railway station. That is a blockade too, as well as this one in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So there were three HVO checkpoints that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very briefly, this Motorola that you mentioned, is it the small hand-held radio station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not mention a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned a Motorola several times during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a device.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Motorola is a trademark. It can imply anything so what I am asking is, what do you call a Motorola? What is it you mean when you say Motorola?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, there seems to be a fairly vigorous debate going on between counsel and the witness but I do not think the translators are getting any part of it. I certainly am not. I ask that Mr. Nobilo ask his question and give the witness time to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Please, think of the interpreters, the Prosecution and, of course, the judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am referring to the question put to you by the Prosecution when you spoke of a Motorola. Is it a hand radio station, a portable radio station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You are a professional military man. What is the range of a portable radio station if there is no relay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the model. It depends on the type. Some such radios have 12 kilometres, 8 kilometres; it depends on the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were asked about Mujahedins in Stari Vitez. Were there any Mujahedins in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I do not know whether you know what a Mujahedin is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you. In prison with you was Patkovic Muhamed and Ahmic Cazim. Were they members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were with me in the rear. They worked with me in the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What were their positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muhamed Patkovic was an officer for logistics. Cazim Ahmic was an officer for logistics, communications, organisation of the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that the Muslims did not have free access to the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could Croatian civilians enter the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore civilians could not enter the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was a command-post. It was the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, did the discotheque in the Vitez hotel operate in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the brewery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so, but I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever see Tihomir Blaskic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see him in Vitez ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 15th April, let us take that date, do you know what the deployment of BH-Army units was around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 15th April 1993, let us take the period around that date, do you know, in Vitez municipality, where units of the BH-Army were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the 325th Mountain Brigade of the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did the fighters of this brigade come from and where did the brigade operate in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was a member of the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 15th April 1993, did you have any weapons in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you had to take off your uniform and leave your weapons in the headquarters when you went home to Vitez because it was under HVO control. Why? Why did you have to take your uniform off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I did not dare move around as a member of the TO. I was not allowed to by the HVO. Not just I but no one. Under HVO control, it was prohibited for members of the TO to wear a uniform. Even the Commander himself did not dare go in the area under HVO control because he would be either captured or shot at. We did not dare and we were not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could HVO members walk around in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you think this would be a convenient moment for the break? Are you planning the break now or shall I pass on to a document? Perhaps this might be a suitable moment before I pass on to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly the question that I was going to ask you. Do you still have many questions to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well then, let us have the break as usual and resume at 11.40. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.40 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please bring in the accused. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher for his assistance. I should like a document to be shown to the witness. (Handed). Mr. President, your Honours, unfortunately we do not have the translation into English because during the cross-examination, the need suddenly arose for showing this document. It is very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is no translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: English or French, because we suddenly realised we need this document. It is a brief document and I will read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, any comments? The judge cannot make any comments because we do not have a French translation. What do you think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am in the same position, your Honour; I cannot make any comments about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will have confidence in the Defence and in the interpreters, so we are not going to deprive the Defence of submitting this document during the cross-examination. Mr. Nobilo, please read slowly so that everyone can understand the meaning and the impact of this document. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me just remind the court that we ended with the statement, before the break, made by the witness that he was not allowed to wear uniform as other members of the BH-Army were not allowed to wear uniforms, whereas HVO people could wear uniforms. The document in the heading says: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Defence Council, the Command of the Viteska Brigade. Defence military secret, strictly confidential." The number is 01/117/93; Vitez, 8th April 1993. Heading: "Prohibition of movement of uniformed persons wearing arms in inhabited areas." The text: "Due to the frequency of disturbances of public law and order, murders, wounding, threats with force of arms, opening fire on settlements, as well as due to the deterioration of the overall security situation, on the basis of the orders of the Commander, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, I hereby order: "(1) in all inhabited areas and roads, the movement of persons wearing uniforms and carrying weapons should be prohibited if military personnel are not performing official duty, except in the course of their departure for the battle front or their return from the frontlines; "(2) officers of the HVO military police shall be obliged to disarm all armed men, to make a record of the weapons and store it in the brigade warehouse, and report to the command of the same; "(3) in the event of opposition, the person shall be taken to the premises of the military police, a statement shall be taken from him, and, if necessary, he shall be remanded in custody and charges placed against him with the corresponding military court; "(4) short-barrelled weapons (pistols, revolvers and the like) may be worn by persons only with the appropriate permits, and long-barrelled weapons by members of the military police and the civilian police. "(5) This order shall be carried out in inhabited areas and communication lines by seeking IDs and searching individuals and M through V" -- I am not aware of what that means, probably motor vehicles. "(6) Any person who opens fire in inhabited areas without authorisation shall be immediately captured, disarmed, regardless of any permit, and charges brought against that person to the competent commander. "(7) All subordinate commanders shall be held responsible for the implementation of these orders." Signed: Commander of the Brigade, Mario Cerkez. Copies submitted to the Commander Anto Bertovic, to the commanders of independent units, one copy to the Commander of the military police and one copy to the archives or the records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, so obviously this exhibit needs to be translated into English and French.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It will be done subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, have you heard of an order of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now that you have seen it, do you still claim that only members of the TO could not walk around in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In this order, reference is made only to units of the HVO. Where is the TO staff? Does it exist here? Has the order been issued that no one should move around in uniform outside his working place? Is there any mention of the TO staff in Vitez? How can I know that the HVO gave these orders that I am not allowed to move around in uniform when it was not submitted to the TO staff at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did you not tell us a moment ago that you knew that you were not allowed to move around in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew as far as I personally was concerned. We all knew, because the HVO disarmed only Muslims, not Croats. Croats could carry long-barrelled guns. How is that, if I as a Muslim was not allowed to carry such guns according to these orders -- how is it possible that HVO and Croats could carry such weapons? Not just the police, but many other people outside the police. I knew this as far as I personally was concerned, and I apologise to the court, but I must explain. Your Honours, I have to explain something a moment ago when I was asked by Mr. Nobilo regarding my job, the duties I performed. I do not agree, I was head of the transportation service, but only for the municipal staff of Vitez; that is for the town. I was not head of the whole transportation service. I only had four vehicles, and I was not responsible for the rest of the transportation. I have to explain this, so that it should not be understood that I was responsible for transportation as a whole. I was responsible only for the town of Vitez. As for other transportation, that was not my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, the court thanks you for this clarification which I think you made clear already during your testimony. We have all understood that you had four vehicles. Now let us go back to the question of Mr. Nobilo. Have you finished with that question or do you wish to continue? I think the witness has answered. Do you wish to pursue that question further? You can put it in some other way. If not, please proceed to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one more question. Despite these orders, you saw HVO members in uniform and carrying long-barrelled guns. Does that mean that the order was not respected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In connection with the statement that you just made on your own initiative regarding the municipal TO, was it responsible for the town of Vitez or the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the town of Vitez, not the municipality. The municipality is something else and the TO for Vitez applies only to the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why was it called the municipal staff of TO if it is not responsible for the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know; do not ask me that. I do not know how to answer that question, why it was called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that there was tension on the 15th and the city was blocked. In your Territorial Defence headquarters, did you receive any information in that connection, in terms of mounting tension or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day, the gentlemen from the HVO and the army had a meeting at the fire brigade building in Mahala. The atmosphere was normal, they talked, I do not know what they were talking about. I completed my work and I went home. When I came back, I heard that my Commander came in. He said, "It is over, the meeting. I had a meeting." I asked him with whom and he said he had a meeting with the HVO. That was on the 15th. Then I went home. However, nobody told me a thing and I did not know anything, believe me. I did not know what was going on, I just knew that I had to change in order to get home safely. This was for the sake of my personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the TO headquarters, were senior officers on duty all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not really understand your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the day of the 15th or the night between the 15th and 16th April 1993, in the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, were there senior officers who were on duty and was this extraordinary? Were they on duty all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez, do you know how many soldiers there were in the night before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence in Stari Vitez have a military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had 13 military policemen, something like that. At any rate, I know there were 13 military policemen in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was civilian police. I do not know how many of them, but there was a civilian police, and after they were moved out of the MUP by the HVO, they were located up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As concerns the tensions that you noticed: did you know that Zivko Totic, the Commander of the HVO brigade from Zenica, had been abducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know Darko Kraljevic the Commander of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear about the ambush that the BH-Army had laid for him near Vitez on 13th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 13th April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Two or three days before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear about the attack on Darko Kraljevic in Novi Travnik on 12th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic was attacked in Novi Travnik? I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear about the abduction of four officers, HVO officers, in Novi Travnik on 13th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear about the burning of ten Croatian flags in Travnik, in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you mentioned that you came with that van of yours, when you were arrested, and when there was a roadblock in Ahmici, you mentioned that you arrived in the village of Mostre. Where is Mostre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Near Visoko? How far away from Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, perhaps 500 metres away or a kilometre away; I cannot tell really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you saw this tense situation, you said that you went for a walk with your wife.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the reason for doing this, in order to observe the situation or just for the sake of going for a walk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to see what was going on in town. I did not understand what was going on in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you realised what was going on in town, did you report your observations to the TO headquarters in Vitez because you were a military person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have any way of reporting because I was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A telephone where there was HVO command? No Muslims could have telephones that day from 10.00 to 3.00 or at other times, only a certain number of Croats in Vitez had access to telephones. Nobody else, all other telephone lines were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, did you consider yourself to be a military man or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You described mortar shelling on the 16th. Did you hear any other shooting, any other signs of a battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did; they were shooting all over the place. It is very hard to tell. I could watch the place where the shooting was going on. I could not see a great deal, but there was a lot of shooting going on and it was very loud, but from what sides, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was Vitez shelled on the 16th, the part that was held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- no, I do not think so. I do not know what you are actually referring to, what positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The positions of the HVO in Vitez: were they shelled by artillery or mortars on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father-in-law lived in the centre of town, so there was shooting, but I do not know whether it was shelling. I cannot tell, because the lines were removed -- they were not in the centre of town where my father-in-law lived, so I did not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 17th April, was Vitez shelled then, a day later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 18th and 19th until you were arrested, was Vitez shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I lived, in that part of town, there were not any shells, but I heard -- people told me that shells fell near the pharmacy and elsewhere. I heard about this from people, Croats, from when I was still there until I was taken to the SDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please help us, the pharmacy, is that the part of Vitez which was under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Above the SDK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not above the SDK, next door to a cafe which is called Benz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a siren that went off in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the sirens were alerted, two or three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Again I wish to draw your attention to something. You are a military man. Can you recognise signals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were sirens of general danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that together with you there were people from the age of 12 onwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hrustipasic Edin was 12 years old, together with his brother who was about 19. Hrustipasic Muharem and Hrustipasic Enver, their father. The three of them were from the same building that my father-in-law lived in. I only knew my father-in-law and the neighbours who lived next door; they knew that I was his son-in-law so when they were taken away, this 12-year-old boy was taken away too. His mother cried and she tried to explain, but this colleague of mine said that he would have to come along with us, that he would be safer in the SDK than over there, but the other thing proved to be true, that it was not safer at the SDK rather than at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your departure to the SDK, was this a service that your friend did to you? How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a way, it was a service, but in a way, it was also forcible. You know, when you dare not stay some place because -- if you know that you will be arrested, that you will be taken away from that place, somebody who does not know you will come and there will be problems, but then on the other hand, if you look at it, if this is a friend of mine, he is going to protect me, so this colleague of mine helped me in one way, but in this other way in which he could not help me, it is not his fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you informed that you were the person they were looking for because you were a TO officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did have such information. This colleague of mine told me that too. He guarded the building. You know, Vitez is a small town and we all knew each other there. Everybody knew about me, that I worked in the Territorial Defence, that I was a member of the Territorial Defence, so that was a major reason for being afraid, knowing that people from all quarters came into the town of Vitez. I was not afraid of the people who knew me from Vitez, but I was afraid of those people who did not know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The young boy aged 12, was he in the SDK all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was at the SDK all the time. He did not go anywhere. He did not go out to dig trenches, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now we have come to the digging of trenches. You showed us where trenches were dug and now I am trying to ask you to try to reconstruct where HVO lines were. I am going to place a map on the easel now, so let us try to see where HVO lines were, what you saw on the left-hand side and the right-hand side, and where did the people from the BH-Army see you from and where did they possibly shoot from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an identical map to the one we had before, that is to say made by the JNA, 1 to 50,000, and this is a general map that was used in the former Yugoslavia, in the JNA, the TO, et cetera. Let us move on to Kratine, please. You said that you saw four HVO units in a defence line. In your opinion, where did they hold this defence line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I will not be able to indicate this exactly on a map. I cannot say exactly whether it was here, but approximately over here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If a mark is going to be made on the map it may be more accurate if the witness marks the map instead of counsel, because I think the witness is in the best position to make the marks on the map. I would ask that that be the modus operandi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please draw the line where it was. I think you can see this approximately. To the left-hand side and to the right-hand side, as far as you could see, so you were not only digging trenches but you could also see these lines. Thank you. Could you tell us now, as opposed to that, at what distance were BH-Army lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This part is covered by forest (indicates). There is a forest here, and here you can see it, but they were in Kuber, here. All of this is Kuber. I cannot tell exactly what the distance is, that is impossible, but in these clearings, I could personally see it, for example here (indicates), the line is about 2 kilometres away. I am not sure because I could not really count, so, as far as the Territorial Defence is concerned, that is what I can approximately say. I do not know what the distance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you approximately show us where Kuber is, which part was held by the BH-Army. Just approximately; it is not that important at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over here (indicates). It is hard to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the left-hand side and on the right-hand side from this area; who held what? Did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not really watch because we all had to do what we were told. We did not have much time to think who was left and who was right, but this is the only thing I could see. When I went to dig here, for example, the Jokers were on the left and another unit was there, I do not know exactly which one, and then on this part over here, this is where the Jokers were for example on the left-hand side. Then when we built part of the -- when we dug part of the trenches they needed, they -- we moved on to the MUP part. That is where we were guarded by a person from the MUP and then we were supposed to go and cut the forest further for the military police. Then we were covering dugouts for the military police and we finished by working for the HVO, and Ivica was there. He was realistic, he was very kind to us; he even allowed us to smoke a cigarette. He simply did not behave like the rest of them, and that is how I managed to see which unit it was, because when I was working for the Jokers I was guarded by a Joker guard, and then, when I went to dig further on, then I was guarded -- not only I but all the rest of us were guarded by one of their men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This first location, can you show me where HVO positions were there at Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which way were they facing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up here. They were facing Kruscica; I do not know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you indicate where the BH-Army was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not see that. You can see it in the other picture. There is a forest there, and our person told us, "Your people are out there and if you start running away, they will start shooting at you too", so we were just digging those trenches and I really do not know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But in what direction did he show when he said, "Your people are over there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They showed this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you mark it please?
